title: Load shedding reassurance scripts
content:
Purpose and audience:
This is a compact playbook of customer-facing language and internal talking points for controlled load shedding (aka deliberate capacity shedding, graceful degradation) across Redwood-hosted and Dedicated deployments. Audience: GTM reps, CS managers, support on-call, and product marketing when drafting status messages.

Executive summary (single-sentence):
When we intentionally reduce feature fidelity or route traffic to lower-capacity regions, we present a short, honest explanation, an expected user impact, an action-oriented mitigation, and a clear timeline. The objective is to keep product teams confident and customers informed, while highlighting Redwood’s engineered fallbacks and multi-region safety nets.

Key principles (for all channels):
- Plain language: avoid jargon like "throttling" without context; use "temporary reduced throughput" or "reduced response fidelity" when relevant.
- Impact-first: lead with what the customer will see (slower responses, shorter completions, model switching).
- What we’re doing: describe the fallback (e.g., routing to model-A-lite, enabling prefix cache, falling back to regional replica).
- What customers can do: reveal simple workarounds (retry, lower max_tokens, pin a model variant, switch region).
- Commitment and timeline: give an ETA or rolling updates cadence and next update time.
- Signal trust: call out auditability (request IDs, trace links) and offer dedicated follow-ups for affected accounts.

Recommended short scripts (for status UI / in-product banner):
1) Minimal (public banner / low-verbosity):
"We’re temporarily reducing throughput in [region] to preserve overall service quality. You may observe slower responses or shorter outputs. We expect normal performance to return within ~X hours. See status.redwood.ai for updates."

2) Technical (developer console + support ticket):
"Incident: load mitigation active in [region] — non-critical requests may be routed to a reduced-capacity model variant. Impact: increased latency and more frequent truncated completions for requests >Y tokens. Mitigation: server-side autoscaling and model-variant fallback are in progress; suggested customer steps: reduce batch sizes and avoid long single-turn generations until resolution. ETA for next update: T+15m."

3) Enterprise SLA notice (email/high-touch):
Subject: Temporary degraded throughput — steps we’re taking
Body: We’re contacting affected teams directly. Summary: To preserve availability across accounts, we have initiated a controlled load-shedding policy in [region]. What you may see: slower responses and occasional truncation for very long requests. What Redwood is doing: routing non-critical traffic to a lower-cost model variant, enabling KV prefix caching, and activating cross-region spillover for high-priority traffic. What you can do: pin mission-critical routes to Dedicated capacity or enable synchronous fallback to another region (we can coordinate). We will follow up at [time]. Private customers: we can open a dedicated channel with an estimated recovery plan.

Customer support quick-reference (L1):
- Empathize: "Sorry for the interruption — we know this can impact production flows."
- Impact question: "Are you seeing timeouts, truncation, or increased latency?"
- Short script options: (a) "Try lowering max_tokens to reduce chance of truncation." (b) "If your app needs strict latency, we can route your critical routes to Dedicated capacity or a different region."
- Escalate to L2 if customer requests contract-level remediation or SLA credit. Provide request IDs and traces.

Sales / AE talking points (prospective/renewal contexts):
- Differentiate: "Many providers simply fail silently when capacity is constrained. Redwood degrades intentionally and predictably — we route to pre-tested model variants and provide explicit transparency and compensating controls."
- Upgrade path: "If workload is business-critical, Dedicated commitments or VPC/private deployment reduce reliance on public capacity and eliminate noisy-neighbor-related load-shedding."
- Cost vs control framing: "We help you balance unit economics and availability: fallbacks save you from outages but Dedicated gives you deterministic headroom."

FAQ (answers for public docs / CS):
Q: Is any data dropped during load shedding?
A: No customer inputs are dropped. Some requests may be routed to a lighter model variant that produces shorter outputs; every request remains traceable and auditable.

Q: How does Redwood decide which requests get shed?
A: Policies are workload-aware: latency-focused routes and priority tokens get prioritized. Public customers are on a tiered routing policy; dedicated/private customers can configure strict routing priority rules.

Q: Will I be charged differently when a fallback runs?
A: Usage will still be accounted; some fallback paths may change token-cost dynamics (shorter outputs reduce total tokens). For enterprise contracts we’ll surface any billing nuances in post-incident notes.

Technical mapping (for engineering + SRE):
- Fallback vectors: model-variant downgrade (quantized / small-arch), region spillover, reduced-max-tokens enforcement, synchronous-to-async conversion, cache-first responses.
- Observability hooks to surface: per-request model variant tag, route priority, downstream region, KV-cache hit ratio, avg token length during incident, % of requests truncated.
- Customer-visible metadata: include a short code in responses (e.g., X-Redwood-Fallback: model-lite-v2) that support can map to incident notes.

Competitive positioning notes (short bullets for pitch decks):
- Competitor A: opaque rate limiting; customers only see failures. Redwood: graceful degradation + explicit consumer-facing messaging.
- Competitor B: static global limits; Redwood: policy-driven, per-route SLOs and controlled regional spillover.
- Positioning line: "You’ll know when we shift gears — and you’ll have control over how your traffic behaves when we do."

Sample incident narrative (for post-incident one-pager):
Title: Mid-Feb regional load mitigation — summary + customer impact
Timeframe: 2026-02-14 03:24–08:12 UTC
Root cause: sudden cross-tenant synthetic traffic spike in eu-west causing queue growth on multiple serving shards.
What we did: enabled model-variant fallback and spillover throttles; enabled prefix cache eviction policy and expanded dedicated routing to prioritized customers.
Customer impact: 3% of requests in eu-west experienced higher-than-normal latency; 0.2% experienced truncated outputs.
Next steps and remediation: added auto-scale floor for critical shards; expanded synthetic-traffic detection rules and updated canary thresholds.

Escalation ladder & owner matrix (short):
- L1 support: handle customer scripts and templated banners (owner: CS Ops).
- L2 product ops: validate fallback behavior and map to model variants (owner: Product Ops).
- L3 SRE: region-level mitigations and capacity shifts (owner: SRE Lead).
- AE/Customer Success: proactive outreach for affected customers (owner: CS Manager).

Quick templates (copy-paste editable):
- In-product banner (single line): "We’re temporarily running lower-fidelity generation in [region]. You may see shorter outputs; full service returning by [ETA]."
- Support ticket opener: "Hi — we’ve started a region-level load mitigation that may affect your requests. Can you share a trace ID or sample request? We’ll route high-priority traffic and follow up within 30 minutes."

Signals to include in customer updates (what to show):
- Start time, estimated resolution, affected regions, high-level impact (latency/truncation), link to status page and request trace, instructions for mitigation.

Success metrics for the playbook (how GTM measures impact):
- % reduction in inbound severity-2 support escalations during mitigations.
- % of affected enterprise customers contacted within target SLA.
- Post-incident NPS delta for impacted accounts.

Open questions for follow-up (for product + eng):
- Should we include a per-response header for fallback reason by default? Security/privacy tradeoffs?
- How granular should customer-configurable fallback policies be in the Console? (per-route, per-model, token-thresholds)
- Automated billing reconciliation for duration-based fallbacks for enterprise customers?

Appendix: quick checklist for a load-shedding event
- [ ] Publish initial banner + status page with ETA.
- [ ] L1: triage inbound cases and gather trace IDs.
- [ ] L2: verify fallback route mappings and prioritize critical routes.
- [ ] L3: execute cross-region spillover and monitor SLOs.
- [ ] CS: notify top 20 customers, offer immediate mitigation options.
- [ ] Post-incident: publish summary, update runbooks, and create regression alerts.

Notes and tone guidance for writers: keep it calm, precise, and action-oriented. Avoid absolutes ("never", "always") — prefer measurable statements ("We expect", "We are targeting"). When possible, include a single next-update ETA to reduce customer anxiety.
